summary.text: The habitable zone is the range of orbits around a star within which a planetary surface could potentially support liquid water.
The range depends on the star's brightness: at the inner edge a planet's water boils off, and at the outer edge it freezes.
The zone is a key tool in the search for habitable planets because discoveries of exoplanets yield approximate orbital radii.

items.prompt: A planet orbits so close that its star's light, trapped by its atmosphere, boils off its oceans. Where is it relative to the zone?

options.label: Past the outer edge, where light is too weak
Inside the inner edge, where light is too strong
Right in the middle, where the balance is best
Anywhere, since distance does not matter

items.explain: At the inner edge the star's light, trapped by greenhouse gases, boils off the planet's water.

items.prompt: Most habitable-zone planets found so far are heavier than Earth. Does that mean heavy planets dominate the zone?

options.label: Yes, light planets cannot hold an atmosphere there
Yes, the zone only forms around giant stars
No, the zone is mostly home to gas giants
No, heavier planets are simply easier to detect

items.explain: Most such planets are more massive than Earth because massive planets are easier to detect.

items.prompt: Life is known to live deep underground on Earth. Why doesn't the classical zone count it?

options.label: It was defined for surfaces that depend on starlight
It was defined only for planets without water
It was defined before deep life was known on Earth
It was defined for planets bigger than Jupiter

items.explain: The classical concept covers planetary surfaces where habitat depends on stellar energy, and deep biospheres would not be detectable on exoplanets.

items.prompt: At the cold outer edge of the conservative zone, what stops a planet from keeping its water liquid?

options.label: The star's light is too strong for any water
Even the greatest greenhouse effect cannot stop freezing
The planet's atmosphere traps all heat inside
The planet's mass is too small to hold water

items.explain: The outer edge is the maximum greenhouse effect limit, where atmospheric absorption is inadequate to keep water from freezing.

items.prompt: Why do some researchers study moons when thinking about the zone?

options.label: Moons are always warmer than planets
Planet-sized moons there might outnumber planets
Moons are easier to detect than planets
Moons orbit closer to stars than planets do

items.explain: Planetary mass moons in the zone might outnumber planets, which interests the field of moon habitability.

items.prompt: A researcher imagines life using methane instead of water. How would the zone idea change?

options.label: It would stay exactly as it is today
It would shrink to a narrower ring
It would be extended to other solvents at the surface
It would move to the planet's deep interior

items.explain: Other zones have been proposed where non-water solvents could be liquid at the surface, and some astrobiologists suggest extending the concept to solvents such as methane.

paragraphs.heading: Not too hot, not too cold
paragraphs.text: The habitable zone is the band of orbits around a star where a planet's surface might hold liquid water. It is also called the circumstellar habitable zone, or the Goldilocks zone, after the fairy tale in which a girl turns down choices that are too extreme and settles on the one that is just right. Many scientists see liquid water as a must for a planet to be habitable.

paragraphs.heading: Inner and outer edges
paragraphs.text: Where the zone sits depends on how bright the star is and how its light acts on a planet's atmosphere. Near the inner edge, starlight trapped by greenhouse gases boils the planet's water away. Past the outer edge, there is too little starlight even with the atmosphere's help, so the water freezes. Many models add other factors on top.

paragraphs.heading: Cautious and hopeful limits
paragraphs.text: Two different cut-offs can be used. In the conservative zone, the inner edge marks where an overheating planet loses its water, and the outer edge is where the greenhouse effect can no longer stop water from freezing. The optimistic zone is wider, allowing for a star's brightness to change as it ages. Its inner edge is called "recent Venus" and its outer edge "early Mars", based on studies of possible past water on those planets.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea came from
paragraphs.text: The concept first arose in geography in the late 19th century. Edward Maunder may have been the first to use the term habitable zone, in 1913. Su-Shu Huang developed the modern version in papers in the 1950s and 60s, and the name Goldilocks zone appeared in the 1970s. In 1993 James Kasting and colleagues used a simple climate model to work out zones for stars of different brightness.

paragraphs.heading: A tool for planet hunters
paragraphs.text: The zone is useful in the hunt for habitable planets because discovering an exoplanet gives a rough size for its orbit. The Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, was built specifically to find planets in habitable zones. Its data suggest that at least 20%, and maybe 50%, of the stars we can see at night host Earth-sized planets within their own zones. The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite carried on the search in 2018. Most habitable-zone planets found so far are heavier than Earth, because massive planets are easier to detect.

paragraphs.heading: Close to home and beyond
paragraphs.text: Proxima Centauri b, about 4.2 light-years from Earth, is the nearest known exoplanet and orbits in its star's habitable zone. In 2013 astronomers used Kepler data to estimate that up to 40 billion Earth-sized planets in the Milky Way may orbit within the habitable zones of red dwarfs and Sun-like stars. About 11 billion of those may circle Sun-like stars. Moons as big as planets in these zones might even outnumber the planets.

paragraphs.heading: Stretching the idea
paragraphs.text: Some researchers have widened the concept. A galactic habitable zone is the part of a galaxy near enough to the centre for stars to be rich in heavier elements, but far enough away to escape the fierce radiation and gravity found at the centre. Some astrobiologists also suggest zones for other liquids, such as methane or sulfuric acid, that could support life built on a different biochemistry.
